PSI U PERSONALITy OF THE MONTH
Carl Carmer, Psi. '14
By Albert J. Elias, Upsilon '46
THERE
was a time when people were
convinced it should be Cramer. The
man still has his troubles with telephone
operators, salesgirls and the uninitiated.
But others, the majority, which means
practically everyone who has been doing
any reading in the past three decades,
now know that the author's name is quite
rightly spelled Carmer�Carl Carmer.
For surely Carmer has worked in more
media than almost any other top-flight
American writer. As a writer of books he
has turned out the best-selling Stars Fell
on Alabama, Genesee Fever, and The
Hudson�as well as The Submarine Stur
geon, Deep South, and Listen for a Lone
some Drum, to which he is now
writing a
sequel. He has composed for magazines
and newspapers and has been an editor
of Vanity Fair and Theatre Ark. He has
worked in radio, preparing dramatizations
of historical events for the intermission of
the N.Y. Philharmonic broadcasts as well
as for transcription, and creating the more
memorable Taps Is Not Enough for broad
cast on V-E Day. Carmer lectures, too,
and in 1944 delivered the annual Cooper
Union Lincoln address. He has been presi
dent of the Authors' Guild and is now
presiding over the Poetry Society of
America. During the war, he gave his
time to the armed services abroad and for
his "Outstanding and conspicuous service"
was rewarded with enviable citations and
recognition from the O.W.I. ,
the Treas
ury and War Departments, and the Na
tional War Fund, to name only a few.
Before seriously taking pen to paper and
having received degrees from Hamilton
and Harvard, Carmer succumbed to the
teaching profession, as had his mother
and father. He taught creative writing at
Syracuse, Rochester and Alabama univer
sities and it was in Alabama that the
young professor actually started to write.
His first book, a, volume of poems called
Deep South, written in the language of
the southern backwoods, marked the be
ginning of his research into folklore and
legend and was
published in 1932. Critics
called it remarkable for its "skillful ma
nipulation of the ballad form and for the
economy and clarity with which the mono
logues told a succession of curious and de
lightful folktales. It was about peoplepeople observed with unsentimental sym
pathy." And in that way created an un
derstanding of them.
Carmer has fought continually against
ignorance and intolerance�his bond to a
circumscribed group is quite naturally,
then, far less strong than his bond to the
principles of the country in which he lives.
In the eloquent Taps Is Not Enough, a
dialogue in verse in which the Unknown
Soldier of the Second World War is
memorialized, he muses:
"You cannot call this world a
place of peace
Because there are no wars�not while men
work
For less than a
living wage; not while men
find
Too often they are
judged among their fel
lows
By color of their skins and not by texture
Of their minds; not while men starve to
death
While others waste their food; not while men
rule
With purchased power. This man who lies
somewhere
Across the seas, what is his color now?"
When he undertook the series of broad
casts dramatizing American history it was
because he thought American history had
been taught too narrowly. "If America
is to take her proper place in a world
society, we have to understand how our
history was influenced by the things hap
pening across the water. As one of my
characters in the series says at the very
beginning, 'Maybe people might have a
better idea where they're going if they
know where they've been.'
"

years Carmer was a director of the Ameri
can Civil Liberties Union and when it

over the treatment of Lillian Smith's
Strange Fruit in Boston, he aptly described
it as "a new and very dangerous form of
suppression" of an author "as fine and
idealistic a citizen as we have." Shortly
before that incident he further displayed
how all-inclusive is his desire for fair play

He first earned his living as a writer in
New Orleans, working on the Item-Tribune
and running a
press. It was here in New
Orleans, where he had come from the
University of Alabama, that his first,
though privately printed book was
pub
lished�a collection of poems about the
city in which he lived, French Town.
His writings have almost invariably
been about the places in which he has
lived or in which he has done research.
A book may grow out of his preoccupa
tions or, on the other hand, it may be
planned well ahead of the writing. He
does research for discovery as well as for
immediate production. He goes by no
formula or work habit to determine under
which circumstance he will create. Genesee
Fever was an historical novel about a
part
of the country where he had grown up and
about which he knew much. The Hudson,
on the other hand, involved research and
personal contact. For three years he
roamed up and down the Hudson Valley
visiting public hbraries and historical asso
ciations, talking with everyone from shad
fishermen to President Roosevelt; swap
ping yarns with natives and tracking down
bits of gossip and legend. The result was
a
history of the Hudson and its people.
The work habits he abides by are con
fined to a
regimentation of living in order
to get the most produced. He and his
wife, Betty, an illustrator, are
up at 5:30
in their Greenwich Village apartment.
They have a
quick cup of coffee, work
for two hours, breakfast, and then return
to their separate projects. He composes in
longhand on
yellow pads, preferably while
sitting up in bed surrounded by piles of
notes and books. He has fus breakfast in
bed and often stays there for limcheon
and occasionally expects his wife to serve
him even his dinner there.
Carmer, a man of 54 years, has other,
not quite so
worldly passions. Movies, for
instance, appeal to him even when they
are bad; he finds them at theh worst ex
tremely funny. He likes Scotch whiskey,
eight hours of sleep, tennis, dancing ("Ball
room and not ballet"), harness racing,
playing cook on
Sunday. His chief indul
gence: books and clothes. His chief ambi
tion: "To write more and better than I do."
All in all, Carmer has a real grasp of
America�a
country where Carmers first
appeared in 1650. He knows full well
where it's been and he has a
pretty good
idea of where it's going. He is far from
an
inspired writer and he himself admits:
"I know I write well enough to have an
audience. But my work is not as artistic
at it could be." His appeal lies in his
honesty and directness. Yet neither of these
two characteristics alone make a
good
author and Carl Carmer fortunately has
added ingredients of great warmth and
understanding in his writing of the folk
lore and mores of America's past�and the
qualities of a real citizen of his country
in telhng its present and pointing its fu
ture.

NEW MEMBER OF THE EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
OLIVER
B. MERRILL, JR., was born
in Summit, New Jersey, on Novem
ber 13, 1903. He is a son of the late Oliver
B. Merrill, Gamma 1891, a brother of
Lyall and Earl W. Merrill, Gamma 1924
and 1927, and a
grandson of James G.
Merrill, Gamma 1863.
Brother Merrill attended the public
schools in Summit, and Phillips Academy
Oliver B. Merrill, Jr., Gamma '25
at Andover, Massachusetts, from which he
graduated in 1921, being a member of the
Cum Laude Society.
Entering Amherst the following fall in
the Class of 1925, Brother Merrill took an
active part in college activities, as
presi
dent of his class during sophomore year, a
member of the football and basketball
squads, manager of the baseball team, an
editor of the College newspaper and a
member of the Student Council and of
Scarab, the senior honorary society.
In 1928 Brother Merrill graduated from
the Columbia University Law School where
he was a member of the board of editors
of the Columbia Law Review and re
ceived the Ordoneaux Prize for high scho
lastic standing. After a
year in Washing
ton as
secretary to Mr. Justice (later Chief
Justice) Harlan F. Stone, he entered the
office of Sullivan & Cromwell, New York
City, with which law firm he has since
been connected, becoming a member of
the firm in 1937.
During the recent war Brother Merrill
served as Government Appeal Agent of
his local draft board. He also acted as
counsel to the National War Fund, which
conducted national campaigns for funds
for the U.S.O., War Prisoners' Aid and
some sixteen foreign relief agencies during
the war
period.
Brother Merrill has long been active in
Psi U and Amherst affairs. He has been a
member of the Gamma Chapter Corpora
tion since his graduation from college, a
member of the Board of Governors of the
Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon since
1934 and President of the latter from 1942
to 1944.
In 1928 Brother Merrill married Laura
G. Provost, Smith 1926. They reside in
New York and have one daughter, Bar
bara, a student at the Shipley School in
Bryn Mawr.

By Henry C.
TO
Brother Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi
'93, former President of the Executive
Council and Patron Saint of the Archives,
we are indebted for a
copy of Michigan
and the Cleveland Era, a 372 page book
of which he was an editor (and no doubt
sponsor as he was of The Annals of Psi
Upsilon, published in 1941). This book is
about Michigan's great men, graduates
and faculty members, who showed how
one small college, at what is now a rela
tively early period in American history,
provided a
generous measure of leader
ship in a
variety of important public func
tions. A wonderful recital for all Psi U's!
Your Archivist has read this book with
biographical and extreme fraternal inter
est. In fact, he has looked up every likely
Psi U name in the Twelfth General Cata
logue of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity�1917�
which contains all names of Psi U's, living
or dead, as of that date. Psi U names in
the book, of course, are rather frequent,
for our Brothers of that day, as before and
since, had distinguished accomplishments.
To get things really started at Michigan,
after formation of the Phi in 1865, Brother
James Burrill Angell, Si^ma '49, was
ap
pointed President in 1871. He soon be
came an
outstanding representative of
Michigan in the eyes of the nation be
cause of his courses on international law
and political science. For this distinction
he became in 1880 minister plenipotentiary
and extraordinary to China, following the
similar designation to that honor the year
before of Brother Andrew Dickson White,
Beta '53, President of Cornell University.
This was one of the first entrances of uni
versity executives and teachers in the then
new field of diplomacy. And! of course,
they were both Psi U's.
Brother Angell had four diplomatic ap
pointments which are an
important and
honorable record in the history of this
country's foreign relations. Briefly: nego
tiations of treaties with China, tentative
settlements of the North Atlantic fisheries
disputes, a
deep waterway from the Great

Lakes to the sea, and his ministry to
Turkey which led to reforms in the treat
ment of American Missionaries when senti
ment was hostile to them.
A truly amazing person, to a latter day
reader, is Brother Lawrence Maxwell, Phi
'74. I'll cite his avocation before his voca
tion, for we Psi U's seem to live by our
extracurricular activities. Brother Maxwell
was one of the founders of, and until his
death, one of the dominant, creative and
leading members of the Cincinnati May
Festival Association. He was made Presi
dent in 1905 and held that office until his
death in 1927.
Brother Maxwell's vocation was the law.
Ten years after graduation from Michigan
he argued his first case before the United
States Supreme Court. Nine years later he
was
appointed Solicitor General of the
United States, succeeding Charles H.
Aldrich, Phi '75, "one of the most bril
liant lawyers in Chicago in his time." Upon
the death of Brother Maxwell, the Cincin
nati Enquirer said: "a man of high attain
ments embodying all the romance and
culture that are associated with the pro
fession of the law. He was one of the fore
most lawyers in the country, and became so
prominently associated with cases involv
ing Federal constitutional and legal ques
tions that interest in his appearances often
overshadowed the issues at bar."
As I proceed through the pages, I
find there are also some
good men in the
Cleveland Era who, while not Psi U's,
were much admired by us. Brother Wil
liam D. McKenzie, Phi '96, was the co
author of the sketch of J. Sterling Morton,
a Chi Psi, who had he not been expelled

would have graduated in 1854. Mr. Mor
ton established Arbor Day in 1872 and in
1893 was
appointed Secretary of Agricul
ture. Following along to the next person
ality is another Chi Psi, Thomas Witherell
Palmer, '49, who after being U. S. Senator
from Michigan, Minister to Spain, etc.,
presented Palmer Park to Detroit. The

many

months and years of great anxiety, follow

more

much comfort from Brother McLaughry's
first-hand memories of the last days of
their only son�a
privilege not shared by
many families who lost loved ones with the
Maruie Corps and Navy.

experience might well serve as a fine ex
ample for surviving brothers to check the
long lists of "Missing and Killed," pre
viously printed in The Diamond, on the

past presi
